hero.h1: From a rack to an atom. 800 million times closer.
hero.lede: Zoom into a real AI chip, level by level. At every level, explore how it works, build something, break it, or imagine what comes next.
hero.map.label: Die view
hero.map.note: This die is also the map of the lab: each block is one layer you can explore, and some zoom further down. Pick a block.
hero.gate.label: Gate
hero.gate.note: Off: the gate squeezes all three sheets shut, so no current flows. Older, flat transistors still leaked here.
hero.hook.1: 72 GPUs, cabled so they act like one giant computer.
hero.hook.2: Liquid, not air: cold plates carry the heat off every chip.
hero.hook.3: 336 billion transistors and 288 GB of memory in one package.
hero.hook.4: As big as one flash of light can print: about 26 × 33 mm.
hero.hook.5: Tensor cores do almost all of the AI math.
hero.hook.6: Every gate is a ready-made cell, wired on stacked copper layers.
hero.hook.8: Three sheets about 5 nm thick, gripped on every side.
hero.hook.9: Only about 20 atoms thick. That is why shrinking is so hard.
hero.why.1.build: A rack exists to answer questions cheaply. Design the chip that does it.
hero.why.1.break: At this scale, one chip in thousands quietly giving wrong answers becomes a daily problem.
hero.why.1.imagine: The future of AI may be decided by electricity as much as by chips.
hero.why.2.build: One tray holds several kinds of chip, each picked for a different job.
hero.why.2.break: Every part on this board crossed borders to get here. Break one link.
hero.why.2.imagine: New chips start as companies. Can yours reach first silicon?
hero.why.3.build: Pick the dies, memory stacks and package for the biggest chip you can make.
hero.why.3.break: Two dies and eight memory stacks: one bad part can waste the whole package.
hero.why.3.imagine: What if the whole model lived on one giant wafer instead of in memory stacks?
hero.why.4.build: Your own design can end up on a real die, on a shared community chip.
hero.why.4.break: Every die is tested before it ships. How much testing is enough?
hero.why.4.imagine: Does the future even look like this die?
hero.why.5.build: Add your own instruction to a real open processor. That is how AI chips begin.
hero.why.5.break: AI now helps design blocks like this one. Can you tell when it is wrong?
hero.why.5.imagine: What if the math happened inside the memory, with no data moving at all?
hero.why.6.build: Place and wire your own cells. Too tight and the wires no longer fit.
hero.why.6.break: Signals take time to cross these wires. Push the clock until it breaks.
hero.why.6.imagine: Blind evolution sometimes finds circuits no engineer would draw.
hero.why.7.build: Cells like this one become the processor you program later.
hero.why.7.break: One wrong connection in one cell, copied a billion times.
hero.why.7.imagine: Could a machine design the cells themselves?
hero.why.8.build: Try the gate switch on the picture first: on, current flows; off, it should stop completely.
hero.why.8.break: No two of these switches are exactly alike, and they wear out with use.
hero.why.8.imagine: CFET stacks the two kinds of switch on top of each other. 2D materials may come after that.
hero.why.9.build: Every chip starts as one flawless crystal. Grow it yourself.
hero.why.9.break: Physics sets a minimum energy for every bit. Try to cheat it.
hero.why.9.imagine: Today we are far above the floor. How close could a future machine get?

map.aboutText: Open Silicon Lab is an open-source project about every kind of chip, from the microcontroller in a thermostat to the GPUs in an AI data center. It is made with AI: Claude wrote the text, simulations and code with the project owner, from public sources. Every simulation is a teaching model; each one says what it simplifies. Facts carry their source and the date they were last verified, and are rechecked every month.

wi.simplifiesText: A teaching model, not a forecast. Each rule says which way one thing pushes another, and the directions follow the economics and the events of 2021–2026 below. The strengths are illustrative round numbers. The real industry has delays, feedback loops (higher prices cool demand; shortages pay for new fabs that later end them), stockpiles, contracts and politics, which this model leaves out. Effects are shown as changes from today, all at once.

cz.label: Your chip, from the demo board down to one transistor. Use the level buttons, the slider or Zoom in.
cz.tipCell: Select a cell to open it at the next level.
cz.tipFet: Select a transistor to zoom into it.
cz.tipFlop: That is a flip-flop: it holds one bit between clock ticks. Memory and the clock shows what is inside one.
cz.shape.180: a flat (planar) transistor with a polysilicon gate
cz.shape.130: a flat (planar) transistor with a polysilicon gate
cz.shape.28: a flat (planar) transistor with a metal gate on a high-k insulator
cz.shape.3: stacked silicon sheets with the gate wrapped all around them
cz.level.board.name: Demo board
cz.level.board.d: A demo board like Tiny Tapeout's: switches set your chip's inputs and LEDs show its outputs. A small helper microcontroller picks which design on the shared chip is switched on.
cz.level.pkg.name: Package
cz.level.pkg.d: With the lid off: thin gold bond wires join the pads around the edge of the silicon die to the package's pins, which are soldered to the board.
cz.level.die.name: Shared chip
cz.level.die.d: One die shared by {tiles} tiles, each a different person's design. Yours is the outlined one. Sharing the masks is what makes a chip cost a few hundred dollars instead of millions.
cz.level.die.d28: Commercial shuttles share one die between many {node} designs too, but a slot costs far more and the design kits are not open. Yours is the outlined one.
cz.level.die.d3: At 3 nm there are no shared shuttles like this: only companies that pay for a whole mask set make chips. This shows where your design would sit if there were one.
cz.level.tile.name: Your tile
cz.level.tile.d: Your tile is about {tw} × {th} µm at {node}. Your design, {cells} cells in {w} × {h} µm, fills about {share}% of it: there is room for far more.
cz.level.design.name: Your design
cz.level.design.d: {cells} standard cells placed in rows by simulated annealing, joined by {wires} µm of wire on two metal layers with {vias} vias between them. Bright wires carry a 1, dark ones a 0.
cz.level.cell.name: One cell
cz.level.cell.d: Your {type} cell opened up: {n} transistors. The p-type ones on top connect the output to 1, the n-type ones below connect it to 0, and the inputs make sure exactly one side conducts.
cz.level.fet.name: One transistor
cz.level.fet.d: This {kind} in your cell is {state}. At {node} it is {shape}; its gate is roughly {len} long. The voltage on the gate opens or closes the channel between source and drain.
cz.note: Built from your design with the same engines as the labs: the cells, their places, the wires and every value on them are computed, and the tests check that each cell's transistors give the same answer as its logic. Simplified: the board, package and shared chip are drawn in general terms (a Tiny Tapeout-style chip of 160 tiles; tiles drawn at Tiny Tapeout's SKY130 size, scaled with the process), a cell is drawn as its circuit inside its real outline rather than as its masks, and the transistor is a sketch, not to scale in depth.

zoom.1.name: AI rack
zoom.1.d: A rack-scale AI system in the class of NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72: 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs on trays, cabled so they behave like one giant computer. Liquid cooling pipes run down each side. Shipping from the second half of 2026.
zoom.2.name: Compute tray
zoom.2.d: One slide-out tray seen from above. GPU packages, a CPU, its memory, power stages and connectors sit on a circuit board under liquid-cooled cold plates.
zoom.3.name: GPU package
zoom.3.d: Two reticle-size compute dies sit side by side on a silicon interposer, flanked by eight HBM4 memory stacks. The whole package holds 336 billion transistors and 288 GB of memory.
zoom.4.name: Compute die
zoom.4.d: One die is about 26 × 33 mm, the largest area a scanner can print in one exposure. It is tiled with identical processor blocks (streaming multiprocessors) around a shared cache band.
zoom.5.name: Streaming multiprocessor
zoom.5.d: One processor block, about 3 mm across. Amber blocks are tensor cores, the matrix engines that do almost all AI math. Cyan banks are register files; the violet band is fast on-chip SRAM.
zoom.6.name: Standard-cell rows
zoom.6.d: Logic is laid out as rows of standard cells, each a pre-designed gate such as NAND or a flip-flop. The colored lines are copper wires on stacked metal layers that connect them.
zoom.7.name: One logic cell
zoom.7.d: A cell as a layout engineer sees it. Red vertical lines are gates about 48 nm apart. Green strips are transistor channels (p-type above, n-type below). Grey rails carry power.
zoom.8.name: Nanosheet transistor
zoom.8.d: A cut through one gate-all-around transistor: three silicon nanosheets, each about 5 nm thick, fully wrapped by the gate metal (amber) and a thin insulator (violet). Electrons flow from source to drain when the gate is on.
zoom.9.name: Silicon atoms
zoom.9.d: The channel is a silicon crystal with atoms 0.235 nm apart. A 5 nm nanosheet is only about 20 atoms thick, which is why further shrinking is so hard and new materials are being studied.
